raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old female patient with no previous medical history presented to the emergency department with sudden onset, sharp epigastric pain that started 12 hours prior, with a level of pain ranging from seven to 10 (on a scale of 0-10) without any associated symptoms. The patient was an immigrant from Mexico who came to the United States several years ago and had no history of recent travel outside the United States and no contact with pets. On presentation, the patient's temperature was 96.3 degrees Fahrenheit, her heart rate was 58 beats per minute, and her blood pressure was 118/63 mmHg. On examination, the patient had scleral icterus and mild tenderness in the epigastric and left upper quadrant. Significant laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 11.1(K/microL) with an absolute neutrophil count of 64%, a lymphocyte count of 12%, an eosinophil count of 19%, a bilirubin level of 2.5 mg/dL, aspartate transaminases of 527 mg/dL, alanine transaminases of 333 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase of 44 mg/dL, and lactate of 3.0 mmol/L.
The laboratory findings are shown in Table 1 below.
A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen revealed a 4.5 x 2.8 cm water density lesion in the right lobe of the liver, with surrounding enhanced margins at segment six of the liver suspicious of a liver abscess or an infected cyst (Figure 1).
She was started on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam at 3.375 g every six hours (3.375 g IV q6hr), and interventional radiology performed percutaneous aspiration and drain placement, considering the concern for abscess. The patient tolerated the procedure well and experienced no complications. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures of the fluid did not yield any organisms. The patient remained afebrile and had no associated leukocytosis after starting the antibiotics. The cytology of the drained fluid revealed mixed inflammation, degenerative debris, and background-scattered retractile hooklets with a few protoscolices. The microscopic studies of the cytological fluid demonstrated protoscolices and hooklets. These features are compatible with hydatid cysts (Figures 2-4).
The patient was started on albendazole 400 mg twice daily. The CT-scan imaging did not reveal any involvement of the other organs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen revealed a second cyst, and the staging of the main cyst was classified as CE3B. Puncture-aspiration-injection-respiration (PAIR) was not available at our facility; therefore, the drain was removed and surgery was consulted. Echinococcal serology results were positive.
The patient underwent a laparoscopic partial hepatectomy. She was found to have scattered nodules in the peritoneum with concern for seeding, given her recent aspiration and drain placement. A biopsy of the inflammatory nodules in her abdomen revealed no viable organisms. Her postoperative course was complicated by postsurgical hemorrhage of the liver, and the patient underwent exploratory laparotomy with suturing of the bleeding and hematoma evacuation. She subsequently recovered and was discharged on oral albendazole 400 mg twice daily for six months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of sudden-onset, severe sharp epigastric pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute, sharp epigastric pain rated 7-10/10 in severity 12 hours prior to emergency presentation, without associated fever, nausea, or vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; immigrated to the United States from Mexico several years earlier with no recent international travel or pet contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe sharp epigastric pain (7-10/10); negative for associated constitutional or gastrointestinal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: temperature 96.3 F, heart rate 58 beats/min, blood pressure 118/63 mmHg. Physical examination revealed scleral icterus and mild tenderness in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed WBC 11.1 K/uL (64% neutrophils, 12% lymphocytes, 19% eosinophils), total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL, AST 527 U/L [reported as mg/dL], ALT 333 U/L [reported as mg/dL], ALP 44 U/L [reported as mg/dL], and serum lactate 3.0 mmol/L. Echinococcal serology was positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 4.5 x 2.8 cm fluid-density lesion with enhancing margins in hepatic segment VI initially suspected to be a liver abscess. Interventional radiology percutaneous aspiration and drain placement yielded fluid with negative aerobic/anaerobic bacterial cultures; fluid cytology and microscopy identified mixed inflammation, degenerative debris, scattered refractile hooklets, and protoscolices. Subsequent abdominal MRI identified a second hepatic cyst and staged the main cyst as WHO CE3b. Laparoscopic partial hepatectomy (with biopsy of scattered peritoneal inflammatory nodules showing no viable organisms) was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Hepatic cystic echinococcosis (WHO stage CE3b in segment VI plus a second hepatic cyst), confirmed by positive echinococcal serology and microscopic identification of protoscolices and refractile hooklets in aspirated cyst fluid. Initially treated empirically with IV piperacillin-tazobactam (3.375 g every 6 hours) and percutaneous aspiration, she was started on oral albendazole 400 mg twice daily and underwent laparoscopic partial hepatectomy (complicated by postoperative hepatic hemorrhage requiring exploratory laparotomy for hemostasis and hematoma evacuation), followed by discharge on a 6-month course of oral albendazole 400 mg twice daily.
